# Local inflammatory responses

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Basics of rheumatology > Local inflammatory responses*

[Original Article Link](/library/aq0QCS)

---

## Summary

Inflammation is the response of vascularized tissues to harmful stimuli such as infectious agents, mechanical damage, and chemical irritants. Inflammation has both local and systemic manifestations and can be either acute or chronic. Local inflammatory response (local inflammation) occurs within the area affected by the harmful stimulus. <u>Acute local inflammation</u> develops within minutes or hours following a harmful stimulus, has a short duration, and primarily involves the <u>innate immune system</u>. The five classic signs of <u>acute local inflammation</u> are redness, swelling, heat, <u>pain</u>, and loss of function. These signs are caused by the sequence of events that is triggered by tissue damage and allows <u>leukocytes</u> to reach the site of damage in order to eliminate the causative factor. This sequence involves changes in local <u>hemodynamics</u> and vessel permeability as well as interaction between <u>leukocytes</u> and <u>endothelium</u> and <u>interstitial</u> tissue, through which <u>leukocytes</u> <u>escape</u> the <u>blood vessels</u>. To sustain the vascular changes and attract more <u>immune cells</u> to the site of inflammation, <u>leukocytes</u> and tissue cells secrete a range of inflammatory mediators, including <u>interleukins</u> and <u>chemokines</u>. Elimination of the causative factor by <u>leukocytes</u> leads to the resolution of <u>acute inflammation</u> and tissue repair with <u>complete regeneration</u> or scarring. Failure to eliminate the causative agent or prolonged exposure to the causative agent leads to <u>chronic inflammation</u>, which confines the causative agent to the site of the initial <u>acute inflammatory response</u>. <u>Chronic inflammation</u> may last months to years and primarily involves the <u>adaptive immune system</u>.

---

## Acute local inflammation

### Overview




* Definition: an immediate response to a pathogenic factor (e.g., trauma, <u>necrosis</u>, foreign bodies, infection)

* Characteristics

* <u>Acute inflammation</u> fulfills the following functions:

* Elimination of pathogenic factor

* Removal of <u>necrotic</u> cells resulting from the initial injury

* Initiation of tissue repair

* Rapid onset (occurs seconds to minutes after an encounter with a causative factor)

* Transient and typically short-lasting;  (i.e., resolves in minutes to days, provided it is not caused by an immunological condition)

* Involves the <u>innate immune system</u> (i.e., the response is not as specific as in <u>chronic inflammation</u>)

* Release of inflammatory mediators leads to the five <u>classic signs of inflammation</u>: see “<u>Classic signs of inflammation</u>” below.

* Inflammatory reaction itself may be harmful to an individual under the following circumstances:

* Excessive reaction (e.g., <u>septic shock</u>)

* Prolonged duration (e.g., persistent <u>tuberculosis</u>)

* Inappropriate reaction (e.g., <u>multiple sclerosis</u>, <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>)





### Involved components




* Cells of the <u>immune system</u>

* <u>Neutrophils</u>, <u>eosinophils</u>, <u>basophils</u>

* <u>Mast cells</u>

* <u>Macrophages</u>

* Peak concentration 2–3 days after the onset

* Predominate in the late stages of <u>acute inflammation</u> (<u>cytokine</u> secretion by <u>macrophages</u> influences the outcome)

* <u>Toll-like receptors</u>

* Inflammasome: <u>cytosolic</u> intracellular multi-protein oligomer of the <u>innate immune system</u> that promotes the initiation of inflammatory responses and induction of pyroptosis (a highly inflammatory form of <u>apoptosis</u> that promotes the maturation, activation, and release of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> and pore-forming <u>proteins</u>) [[1]](/library/1mb2e8)

* Recognition of microbial products, crystals (e.g., <u>uric acid crystals</u>), and products of dead cells

* Activation → cleavage, maturation, and release of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> IL-1β and IL-18 → inflammation and <u>pyroptosis</u> [[2]](/library/WmbPe8)

* <u>Proteins</u>

* <u>Complement</u>

* <u>Antibodies</u> (preexisting)

* <u>Hageman factor</u> (<u>factor XII</u>)

* <u>Arachidonic acid</u> metabolites





### Inflammatory reactions



1. * Local hemodynamic changes (vascular response to injury)

* Initial <u>vasoconstriction</u> is followed by <u>vasodilation</u> → stasis and ↑ blood flow

* <u>Vasodilation</u> is induced by release of the following inflammatory mediators:

* <u>Histamine</u> from <u>basophils</u>, <u>platelets</u>, <u>mast cells</u>

* <u>Serotonin</u> from <u>platelets</u>

* <u>Prostaglandins</u> (<u>PGE<sub>2</sub></u>, PGD<sub>2</sub>, and PGF<sub>2</sub>) from <u>leukocytes</u>, <u>platelets</u>, <u>endothelial</u> cells

* Bradykinin;  (an inflammatory mediator that increases vascular permeability and causes vascular dilation and bronchoconstriction ) from plasma

* <u>Nitric oxide</u> (NO) from <u>endothelial</u> cells
2. * Increased vascular permeability

* Inflammatory mediators (<u>histamine</u>, <u>serotonin</u>, <u>bradykinin</u>, and <u>leukotrienes</u> C<sub>4</sub>, D<sub>4</sub>, and E<sub>4</sub>) rapidly trigger the <u>retraction</u> of <u>endothelial</u> cells →  opening of interendothelial spaces and short-lasting paracellular leakage of plasma

* <u>Endothelial</u> injury → <u>endothelial</u> cell <u>necrosis</u> and detachment → long-lasting leakage until the damaged area is thrombosed or repaired

* Leakage of plasma content → <u>edema</u> and promotion of migration of <u>immune cells</u> and <u>proteins</u> to the site of injury or infection
3. * Cellular effects

* Leukocyte extravasation: <u>Leukocytes</u> (predominantly <u>neutrophils</u>) exit <u>postcapillary venules</u>, accumulate at the site of infection or injury, and are subsequently activated (see “<u>Chemotaxis and leukocyte extravasation</u>”).

* <u>Phagocytosis</u> and killing of the <u>phagocytosed</u> <u>pathogen</u> or lysis of the <u>phagocytosed</u> particles (see “<u>Phagocytosis and killing</u>”)




![Neutrophils in acute inflammation](media/rsb4uchwug3ovrytk4b6fr3f.jpg)

Neutrophils in acute inflammation

| <br>Possible outcomes of <u>acute inflammation</u> [[3]](/library/p30Ljf) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outcome | Description | Associated mediators and <u>cytokines</u> |
| Persistent <u>acute inflammation</u> | <br>* <u>Acute inflammation</u> remains active and does neither resolve nor progress to <u>chronic inflammation</u>.<br><br> | <br>* <u>IL-8</u><br><br> |
| Resolution with <u>regeneration</u> | <br><br>* Cellular debris and pathogens are removed by <u>macrophages</u>.<br><br>* <u>Edema</u> is resorbed via lymphatic vessels.<br><br>* Damaged tissue is repaired via <u>proliferation</u> of <u>stem cells</u>.<br><br>* See “<u>Wound healing</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>IL-10</u><br><br>* <u>TGF-β</u><br><br><br> |
| Resolution with scarring | <br><br>* Cellular debris, pathogens, and <u>edema</u> are cleared.<br><br>* There is a lack of <u>stem cells</u> to replace the damaged tissues<br><br>* Original tissue is replaced by <u>fibrotic</u> <u>scar</u> tissue.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Platelet</u>-derived growth factor (<u>PDGF</u>)<br><br>* FGF-2<br><br>* <u>TGF-β</u><br><br><br> |
| Abscess formation | <br><br>* Inflammation → <u>pus</u> formation and tissue <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* The focus of <u>necrosis</u> is separated from healthy tissues by a fibrous capsule.<br><br>* Septic abscess: an <u>abscess</u> that results from infection<br><br>* Sterile abscess<br><br>* An <u>abscess</u> that is not caused by infection<br><br>* May form as a complication of subcutaneous/intramuscular injection when the injected substance (e.g., <u>glucocorticoids</u>, synthol, oils) is not absorbed and causes persistent irritation or as a result of ongoing inflammation in a previously <u>septic abscess</u> after the causative <u>pathogen</u> has been cleared.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* IL-1β<br><br>* <u>TNF-α</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Chronic inflammation</u> | <br><br>* Persistence of causative factor<br><br>* <u>Macrophages</u> and other <u>APCs</u> present <u>antigens</u> to <u>T-helper cells</u> → activation of <u>CD4+ Th cells</u> → infiltration of affected tissues<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>IL-1</u><br><br>* <u>TNF-α</u><br><br>* <u>IL-12</u><br><br>* <u>IL-6</u><br><br><br> |

## Chemotaxis and leukocyte extravasation

### General information




* When tissue is inflamed, <u>leukocytes</u> (mainly <u>neutrophils</u> in early infection) are released from the <u>bone marrow</u> reserve pool into the <u>circulatory system</u>, where they interact with vascular <u>endothelium</u> and leave the <u>blood vessels</u> (predominantly <u>postcapillary venules</u>) to migrate to the site of infection.

* The process of <u>neutrophil</u> extravasation from the blood to the inflamed tissue occurs in 5 steps:
1. * <u>Margination</u>
2. * Rolling
3. * Adhesion
4. * <u>Diapedesis</u>
5. * Migration





### Margination




* Definition: a process by which <u>leukocytes</u> are distributed peripherally along the <u>endothelial</u> surface

* Mechanism: The two main mechanisms that allow for <u>margination</u> are <u>rouleaux formation</u> and dilation of post-<u>capillary</u> <u>venules</u>.

* Rouleaux formation

* The <u>liver</u> releases increased amounts of <u>fibrinogen</u> in response to <u>cytokines</u> released by <u>macrophages</u>, <u>monocytes</u>, and other cells near the site of inflammation.

* Increased <u>fibrinogen</u> → <u>rouleaux formation</u> → <u>neutrophils</u> are pushed against <u>endothelium</u> of the <u>venules</u>

* Dilation of post-<u>capillary</u> <u>venules</u>

* The release of inflammatory mediators results in <u>vasodilation</u> of the post-<u>capillary</u> <u>venules</u>.

* As these <u>venules</u> expand, the <u>velocity</u> of blood flow in these areas slows, causing <u>neutrophils</u> to marginate against the <u>endothelium</u> of the <u>venules</u>.

* The <u>venules</u> are the segment of <u>microvasculature</u> most sensitive to inflammation. Their intercellular <u>endothelial</u> junctions open to allow for the flow of <u>plasma proteins</u> and <u>leukocytes</u> between cells. [[4]](/library/9nYNvp)





### Leukocyte rolling




* Definition: a transient weak interaction of <u>leukocytes</u> with <u>endothelial</u> cells that causes them to move slowly along the blood vessel periphery in areas of inflammation in preparation for adhesion

* Mechanism: mediated by adhesion molecules (selectins)

* On <u>endothelial</u> cells

* P-selectin

* Stored in <u>Weibel-Palade bodies</u>

* <u>Histamine</u>-mediated release within the <u>endothelium</u> in response to inflammation

* E-selectin: released in response to inflammatory mediators such as TNF and <u>IL-1</u>

* Other: GlyCAM-1, <u>CD34</u>

* On <u>leukocytes</u>

* <u>Neutrophils</u> and other <u>leukocytes</u> express Sialyl-Lewis<sup>X</sup> and L-selectin, respectively.

* These molecules transiently bind to and dissociate from <u>endothelial</u> <u>selectins</u>, allowing <u>leukocytes</u> to roll along the vascular wall.

* Deficiency of the adhesion molecule <u>Sialyl-Lewis<sup>X</sup></u> causes <u>leukocyte adhesion deficiency</u> type 2.





### Leukocyte adhesion




* Definition: the firm binding of <u>leukocytes</u> to <u>endothelium</u> prior to migrating out of the vasculature

* Mechanism: mediated by adhesion molecules

* On <u>endothelial</u> cells

* Intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM, also called <u>CD54</u>)

* Vascular adhesion molecule (<u>VCAM</u>, also called <u>CD106</u>)

* Both upregulated by TNF and <u>IL-1</u>

* On <u>neutrophils</u> and <u>lymphocytes</u>

* <u>Neutrophils</u>: lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (<u>LFA-1</u>)

* Belongs to β<sub>2</sub>-integrin family

* Composed of CD18 and CD11a

* Binds to ICAM

* <u>Lymphocytes</u> and <u>monocytes</u> β<sub>1</sub>-integrin (also called <u>VLA-4</u>) binds to <u>VCAM</u>

* Expression of <u>integrins</u> is activated by <u>leukotriene B4</u> (<u>LTB<sub>4</sub></u>) and <u>C5a</u>.

* The deficiency of a CD18 <u>integrin</u> subunit causes <u>leukocyte adhesion deficiency</u> type 1.





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Selectins</u> are molecules that allow <u>leukocytes</u> to select the place of their migration (weak binding), while <u>integrins</u> are molecules that integrate (strong binding) the <u>leukocytes</u> with the <u>endothelial</u> cells.




### Diapedesis (transmigration)




* Definition: the transmigration of <u>leukocytes</u> across <u>endothelial</u> barriers (can occur paracellularly or <u>transcellularly</u>)

* Mechanism

* <u>Leukocytes</u> leave the blood vessel by moving between <u>endothelial</u> cells.

* <u>Neutrophils</u> release type IV <u>collagenase</u>, which dissolves the <u>basement membrane</u> and allows them to exit the <u>interstitial space</u>.

* Requires expression of platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (<u>PECAM-1</u>, also called <u>CD31</u>), an endothelial cell adhesion molecule (<u>ECAM</u>) on <u>neutrophils</u>, <u>endothelial</u> cells, and <u>platelets</u>





### Migration




* Definition: the process by which <u>leukocytes</u> travel through the <u>interstitium</u> to the site of inflammation after leaving the <u>blood vessels</u>

* Mechanism: Occurs via chemotaxis, which is mediated by chemoattractants [[5]](/library/53YiQK)

* <u>Leukotrienes</u>: e.g., <u>LTB<sub>4</sub></u>

* <u>Platelet-activating factor</u> (PAF)

* <u>Chemokines</u>: e.g., <u>IL-8</u>

* Kallikrein: a <u>serine</u> <u>protease</u> enzyme that activates <u>bradykinin</u> and regulates blood pressure

* <u>Complement</u> fragments, e.g., <u>C5a</u>

* Bacterial products (e.g., modified <u>peptides</u> called N-formyl <u>peptides</u>)

## Phagocytosis and killing

### Overview




* Definition

* <u>Phagocytosis</u> is the process by which foreign particles, cell debris, or microbes are engulfed and degraded.

* Cells capable of <u>phagocytosis</u> are <u>phagocytes</u> (e.g., <u>neutrophils</u>, <u>macrophages</u>).

* Mechanism: <u>Phagocytosis</u> involves 3 sequential steps.
1. * Recognition of a target
2. * Engulfment
3. * Degradation or killing of the engulfed particle





### Recognition [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)




* General

* <u>Phagocytes</u> have a number of <u>receptors</u> that allow them to recognize and bind surface molecules of <u>target cells</u> or particles.

* <u>Opsonization</u> facilitates recognition of target particles.

* <u>Phagocyte</u> recognition <u>receptors</u> and their <u>ligands</u>

* <u>Mannose</u> <u>receptor</u>: <u>mannose</u>, fucose, N-acetylglucosamine

* Scavenger <u>receptor</u>: <u>low-density lipoprotein</u>

* Opsonin <u>receptor</u>: <u>Fc</u> fragment of <u>IgG</u>, C3b





### Engulfment [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)



* Mechanism

* The <u>phagocyte</u> forms <u>cytoplasmic</u> extensions (<u>pseudopodia</u>) that surround the target cell or particle.

* The plasma membrane around the engulfed cell or particle separates to form a <u>phagosome</u>.

* The <u>phagosome</u> fuses with <u>lysosomes</u>, forming a phagolysosome.

* <u>Lysosomal</u> content is released into the <u>phagolysosome</u>.




### Killing and degradation [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)




* Oxygen-dependent

* Involves production of <u>reactive oxygen species</u> (see “<u>Respiratory burst</u>”)

* There are a number of diseases associated with defective oxygen-dependent killing, including: 

* <u>Chronic granulomatous disease</u> of childhood: deficiency of <u>NADPH oxidase</u> → lack of <u>superoxide</u> ion → recurrent or persistent infections with <u>catalase-positive</u> organisms (e.g., <u>S. aureus</u>)

* <u>Myeloperoxidase deficiency</u> → recurrent <u>fungal infections</u>

* Oxygen-independent: involves <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes such as acidic <u>hydrolases</u> and <u>lysozyme</u>

---

## Chronic local inflammation

<u>Chronic inflammation</u> may be preceded by <u>acute inflammation</u> and can last for months to years. [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)




* Etiology

* Autoimmune diseases

* Chronic exposure to toxic pathogens and foreign material (e.g., silica)

* Nondegradable pathogens (e.g., foreign material)

* Persistent infections (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>syphilis</u>, certain virual and fungal infections) → <u>type IV hypersensitivity reaction</u>

* Cells involved

* <u>Mononuclear cells</u>

* <u>Monocytes</u>

* <u>Macrophages</u>

* <u>Lymphocytes</u>

* <u>Plasma cells</u>

* <u>Fibroblasts</u>

* <u>T lymphocytes</u>

* Pathophysiology

* Mononuclear invasion that causes tissue damage on the one hand, but is simultaneously carrying out repair (in form of <u>fibrosis</u> and <u>angiogenesis</u>) on the other

* Interaction of <u>macrophages</u> and <u>T lymphocytes</u> → chronic inflammation

* There are two possible ways of activating <u>macrophages</u>:

* Classical (proinflammatory): mediated by <u>Th1 cells</u> secreting <u>IFN-γ</u>

* Alternative (repair and anti-inflammatory): mediated by <u>Th2 cells</u> secreting <u>IL-4</u> and <u>IL-13</u>

* Outcomes

* Scarring

* <u>Amyloidosis</u>

* <u>Neoplasia</u>, such as:

* <u>Chronic HCV infection</u> → chronic <u>hepatitis</u> → <u>HCC</u>

* <u>H. pylori</u> infection → chronic <u>gastritis</u> → <u>gastric adenocarcinoma</u>

---

## Granulomatous inflammation

### Overview




* Distinct type of <u>chronic inflammation</u> that is characterized by the formation of <u>granulomas</u> in affected tissues

* May be induced by continuous <u>T-cell</u> response

* When the <u>immune system</u> is unable to completely eliminate a foreign stimulus (e.g., persistent <u>pathogen</u>, foreign body, infections such as <u>TB</u>, immune-mediated diseases), the resulting <u>granulomatous inflammation</u> attempts to wall off the foreign substance within <u>granulomas</u> without completely degrading or eradicating it.

* This results in persistent inflammation that ultimately causes organ damage and <u>fibrosis</u>.





### Etiology




* Infections (most common cause)

* <u>Protozoan</u> infections (e.g., <u>schistosomiasis</u>)

* <u>Fungal infections</u> (e.g., <u>histoplasmosis</u>)

* Bacterial infections

* <u>Mycobacteria</u> (e.g., <u>leprosy</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>)

* <u>Bartonella henselae</u> (e.g., <u>cat scratch disease</u>, stellate necrotizing <u>granulomas</u>)

* <u>Listeria monocytogenes</u> (e.g., <u>granulomatosis infantiseptica</u>)

* <u>Treponema pallidum</u> (e.g., <u>tertiary syphilis</u>)

* Immune-mediated diseases

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Crohn disease</u>

* <u>Subacute thyroiditis</u> (de Quervain)

* <u>Primary biliary cholangitis</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u>

* <u>Granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>

* <u>Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>

* <u>Giant cell arteritis</u>

* <u>Takayasu arteritis</u>

* Foreign body exposure

* <u>Berylliosis</u>

* <u>Talcosis</u>

* <u>Hypersensitivity pneumonitis</u>

* <u>Breast implants</u>

* <u>Penetrating trauma</u> with glass, wood, etc.

* Others: <u>chronic granulomatous disease</u>





### Pathophysiology




* <u>Antigen</u>-presenting cells present <u>antigens</u> to <u>CD4+</u> Th cells and secrete <u>IL-12</u> → stimulation of <u>Th cell</u> differentiation into <u>Th<sub>1</sub> cells</u>

* <u>Th<sub>1</sub> cells</u> activate <u>macrophages</u> by secreting <u>IFN-γ</u> → <u>cytokine</u> release from <u>macrophages</u> (e.g., TNF) → formation of <u>epithelioid macrophages</u> and <u>giant cells</u>

* <u>Epithelioid cells</u> secrete <u>TNF-α</u>, which serves to maintain the <u>granuloma</u>.  

* This is the reason why anti-TNF therapy can promote sequestration of <u>granulomas</u> and cause disseminated disease.

* Therefore, every individual considered for anti-TNF therapy has to be tested for <u>latent TB</u> beforehand.

* <u>Macrophages</u> within the <u>granuloma</u> cause ↑ <u>calcitriol</u> activation due to ↑ <u>1α-hydroxylase</u> activity → <u>hypercalcemia</u>





![Pathophysiology of granuloma formation](media/dm6ig6hjdecityj1kpjbqib2.jpg)

Pathophysiology of granuloma formation




### Pathology




* Granuloma: a nodular collection of central <u>macrophages</u>, <u>epithelioid cells</u> (a differentiated tissue <u>macrophage</u> characterized by abundant pink <u>cytoplasm</u>), and <u>multinucleated giant cells</u> surrounded by <u>fibroblasts</u> and <u>lymphocytes</u>, which contain the following structures:

* Schaumann bodies: <u>cellular inclusion</u> bodies consisting of intracytoplasmic <u>calcium</u> and protein with laminar <u>stratification</u> (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>berylliosis</u>)

* Asteroid bodies: star-shaped, eosinophilic <u>inclusion bodies</u> consisting of various lipids (e.g., from <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>foreign body reactions</u>)

* Types of <u>granuloma</u>

* Caseating granulomas

* <u>Granulomas</u> with central <u>necrosis</u>

* Found in infections (e.g., <u>tuberculosis</u>, <u>fungal infections</u>)

* Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation

* <u>Granulomas</u> without central <u>necrosis</u>

* Found in immune-mediated diseases (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>Crohn disease</u>), <u>vasculitis</u>, and foreign body exposure





> [!TIP]
> <u>TNF-α</u> is important for maintaining the <u>granuloma</u>. It is essential to test patients for <u>latent TB</u> before initiating anti-TNF therapy because the drug causes breakdown of the <u>granuloma</u> and can result in <u>disseminated TB</u>.
